g10-mathematics-um5-t1.overview: A circle is the set of points equidistant from a centre — and that single definition generates a wealth of symmetry: equal radii create isosceles triangles everywhere, perpendiculars bisect chords, and equal chords stand equal distances from the centre. This lesson maps the vocabulary and the symmetry theorems that every later circle result leans on.
objectives: Name circle parts precisely: chord, secant, tangent, arc, segment, sector
Prove/use: perpendicular from centre to a chord bisects it
Prove/use: equal chords are equidistant from the centre (and converse)
Use congruent radii to find hidden isosceles triangles
Apply: the line from centre to a chord's midpoint is perpendicular to it
g10-mathematics-um5-t1.simple: Everything on a circle is equidistant from the centre — that distance is the radius, and it's the same in every direction, which is why circles are the most symmetric shape. Vocabulary first: a chord joins two points on the circle (the diameter is the longest chord, through the centre); a tangent touches at exactly one point; a secant cuts through at two; an arc is a piece of rim; a segment is a crust slice (chord + arc); a sector is a pizza slice (two radii + arc). The symmetry facts: drop a perpendicular from the centre onto any chord — it cuts the chord exactly in half (two right triangles, equal hypotenuses, shared leg → congruent). Flip it: the line through the centre and a chord's midpoint must be perpendicular. And equal chords sit the same distance from the centre — like two ladders of the same length leaning against a wall at the same height. Whenever you see two radii to two points, an isosceles triangle is hiding there — the most-used secret in circle geometry.
g10-mathematics-um5-t1.detailed:
Definitions with precision. Circle centre O, radius r: the locus {P : OP = r}. A chord is any segment joining two circle points; a diameter is a chord through O (length 2r, the longest chord — proof: for any chord AB, AB ≤ AO + OB = 2r by triangle inequality). A tangent meets the circle in exactly one point; a secant is a line through two points. The rim between two points is an arc (minor < 180°, major > 180°); a segment is the region between a chord and its arc; a sector is bounded by two radii and an arc.

Bisection theorem. The perpendicular from the centre to a chord bisects the chord. Proof: let OM ⊥ AB. Triangles OMA and OMB are right-angled with OA = OB (radii) and OM shared — RHS congruence — so AM = MB. Converse: if M is the midpoint of chord AB, then OM ⊥ AB (SSS: OA = OB, AM = MB, OM shared → equal angles at M, which must be 90° since they're supplementary). Corollary: the perpendicular bisector of ANY chord passes through the centre — the basis for finding a circle's centre from an arc, and for the circumcentre construction.

Equal chords ↔ equal distances. Chords are equal iff they are equidistant from the centre (distance = perpendicular length). Proof via Pythagoras: half-chord² + distance² = r², so chord = 2√(r² − d²) — one formula encoding the whole theorem. Consequences: as d → 0 the chord → diameter (longest); as d → r the chord shrinks to nothing. Equal chords also cut equal arcs and subtend equal central angles — the three 'equalities' (chord, arc, central angle) travel together.

The isosceles engine. Any two radii to circle points form an isosceles triangle — base angles equal. This is the workhorse of circle proofs: join the centre to the relevant points, mark the equal radii, and angle-chase. Example: chord AB with ∠OAB = 35° → ∠OBA = 35° → central angle ∠AOB = 110°. Exam technique: when a circle problem stalls, DRAW THE RADII — most hidden structure is isosceles.

Tangent perpendicularity (preview of t4): a tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact — because the contact point is the closest point of the line to the centre (any other point on the line is farther than r, by Pythagoras). This gives the classic: two tangents from an external point are equal in length (RHS with the shared external segment and equal radii), forming a kite with angles 180° − θ between them.

g10-mathematics-um5-t1.summary: A circle is a locus of equal radii, making every two-radius triangle isosceles — the key to angle chasing. Vocabulary (arc, segment, sector, secant, tangent) is the shared language for the angle theorems ahead.

g10-mathematics-um5-t2.overview: Circle angle theorems are the crown jewels of Grade 10 geometry: the central angle is twice the inscribed angle standing on the same arc; angles in the same segment are equal; a semicircle angle is always 90°; opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral sum to 180°. Four statements, endless proofs.
objectives: State and prove the centre–circumference angle theorem (2× rule)
Prove angles in the same segment are equal
Apply Thales: angle in a semicircle = 90°
Prove opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral sum to 180°
Combine theorems to angle-chase through multi-step diagrams
g10-mathematics-um5-t2.simple: An inscribed angle has its vertex ON the circle with both sides as chords; a central angle has its vertex AT the centre. Stand them on the same arc: the central one is exactly TWICE as big. Why? Join the vertex to the centre — you've created two isosceles triangles (radii again!), and the exterior-angle theorem doubles everything. Instant corollaries: angles standing on the same arc from the same side are all equal (all half the same central angle) — 'angles in the same segment'; if the arc is a semicircle, the central angle is 180°, so the inscribed one is 90° — Thales' theorem, the right angle hiding in every semicircle; and if a four-pointed shape sits on the circle (cyclic quadrilateral), its opposite angles sum to 180° because the two arcs make a full 360°. The whole lesson is one theorem and three shadows of it.
g10-mathematics-um5-t2.detailed:
Central = 2 × inscribed. Let A, B be on circle centre O, and P on the major arc. Then ∠AOB = 2∠APB. Proof (the standard one): extend PO to meet the circle again at Q. Triangle OPA is isosceles (OA = OP), so ∠OAP = ∠OPA; exterior angle ∠AOQ = ∠OAP + ∠OPA = 2∠OPA. Likewise ∠QOB = 2∠OPB. Add: ∠AOB = 2∠APB. (When O lies outside the angle, subtract instead — same engine.) This is the master theorem; everything below is a one-line consequence.

Same-segment equality. Any two inscribed angles standing on chord AB from the same side subtend the same arc AB, hence both equal ½∠AOB — so they're equal to each other. The locus view: the set of points P with ∠APB constant is exactly an arc through A and B — this is how you construct 'all viewpoints seeing a segment at 60°'.

Thales (angle in a semicircle). If AB is a diameter, the central angle ∠AOB = 180° (straight line), so any inscribed ∠APB = 90°. Converse: if ∠APB = 90° with P on the circle, AB is a diameter (the 90° chord subtends 180° centrally). Practical gem: to find a circle's diameter from a drawn arc, place a right angle's vertex on the arc and slide until its sides cross the arc endpoints — the chord it spans is the diameter. Also: for P INSIDE the circle the angle is > 90°, outside < 90° — the 'angle comparison' trick for point-location questions.

Cyclic quadrilaterals. For ABCD on a circle: ∠A + ∠C = 180° and ∠B + ∠D = 180°. Proof: the two opposite angles subtend the two arcs that together make the full 360°, so each angle is half its arc and the pair halves 360° → 180°. Converse: if a quadrilateral's opposite angles are supplementary, it IS cyclic — a construction and proof tool. Rectangle: cyclic (opposite angles 90 + 90). Isosceles trapezium: cyclic. Parallelogram: cyclic only if it's a rectangle.

Angle-chasing craft: mark the arc each inscribed angle stands on; hunt for the central twin or a same-segment partner; use isosceles radii triangles; deploy the semicircle right angle the moment a diameter appears; close with cyclic-quad supplements or straight-line/angle-sum facts. Every exam circle proof is a chain of 2–4 of these moves — write each step WITH its reason ('∠ = ½∠ at centre, standing on arc BC') because the reason carries the marks.

Fluent circle geometry is arc-spotting plus reason-tagged angle chasing.

g10-mathematics-um5-t3.overview: Rims and slices get their measurements here: arc length and sector area as fractions of the whole circle, in both degree and radian flavours, plus the segment (crust) area found by subtracting a triangle from a sector. These are the formulas that size sprinklers, gears and curved cuts.
objectives: Derive arc length = (θ/360)·2πr and sector area = (θ/360)·πr²
Use the radian versions s = rθ and A = ½r²θ
Find segment area as sector minus triangle
Work backwards from arc/area to find radius or angle
Solve combined perimeter-of-sector problems
g10-mathematics-um5-t3.simple: A 90° slice is a quarter of the circle — because 90/360 = ¼. That's the entire idea: any arc or sector is the fraction θ/360 of the full rim 2πr or full area πr². Arc length: s = (θ/360)·2πr. Sector area: A = (θ/360)·πr². In radians the fractions simplify to s = rθ and A = ½r²θ (θ/2π of 2πr is just rθ — radian formulas are the degree ones with the 360 bookkeeping cancelled). The tricky cousin is the SEGMENT — the crust between a chord and its arc: compute the sector, subtract the triangle formed by the two radii and the chord, done: segment = sector − ½r²sin θ. Watch the classic trap: the PERIMETER of a sector is arc + TWO radii, not just the arc — a closed crust needs its straight sides.
g10-mathematics-um5-t3.detailed:
Proportional reasoning. The circle is uniform: doubling the central angle doubles the arc and the area. So arc fraction = angle fraction: s/(2πr) = θ/360°, giving s = (θ/360)·2πr; and A_sector/(πr²) = θ/360°, giving A = (θ/360)·πr². In radians (Unit 4's payoff): θ/2π of the whole → s = rθ, A = ½r²θ — the formulas from the radian lesson, now with proof. Both pairs describe the same geometry; pick by the angle's unit, and convert if the question mixes them.

Segment (crust) area. The minor segment cut off by chord AB = sector OAB − triangle OAB. Triangle area via two sides and included angle: ½·r·r·sin θ = ½r² sin θ. So segment = ½r²θ − ½r² sin θ (radians) = (θ/360)πr² − ½r² sin θ (degrees). For the MAJOR segment, subtract the minor from πr². If θ > 180° (reflex sector), the same 'sector − triangle' formula still works with the reflex angle — the triangle term goes negative via sin, which is exactly right.

Perimeter of a sector = arc + 2r (the two straight radii close the shape). Common exam: 'given perimeter P and angle θ, find area' — solve r from P = rθ + 2r = r(θ + 2), then A = ½r²θ. Optimization variant: fixed perimeter, maximum area → A(θ) = P²θ/(2(θ+2)²), maximised at θ = 2 rad — a lovely calculus-flavoured result reachable by completing the square at Grade 10 level (or just tested with values).

Reverse work: from s and θ get r = s/θ; from A and θ get r = √(2A/θ); from s and A eliminate r: A = ½rs → r = 2A/s, θ = s²/(2A). These three-givens-two-unknowns relations appear constantly in gear design (pitch-circle arcs), belt drives and curved-cut material estimation.

Accuracy habits: keep π symbolic until the end; state units (length vs area vs angle); sanity-check fractions — a 60° sector MUST be exactly 1/6 of the circle's area. When the angle is given in degrees but you're using sin in a calculator, degree mode is fine — but for ½r²θ the θ MUST be radians. Mixing the two systems mid-problem is the top error source.

g10-mathematics-um5-t4.overview: The final circle theorems handle lines that meet outside or across the circle: the tangent-radius right angle, equal tangents from an external point, the alternate segment theorem (tangent-chord angle equals the angle in the opposite segment), and intersecting chords/secants with their product rules.
objectives: Use: tangent ⊥ radius at the point of contact
Prove and apply: two tangents from an external point are equal
State and use the alternate segment theorem
Apply intersecting chords: PA·PB = PC·PD
Solve combined circle-proof problems chaining all theorems
g10-mathematics-um5-t4.simple: A tangent kisses the circle at one point — and at that exact point it is perpendicular to the radius. That right angle is the master key: tangent problems almost always start by drawing the radius to the contact point. Second fact: from a point outside the circle, both tangent segments to the circle are EQUAL (two right triangles sharing the hypotenuse-to-centre, equal radii → congruent). They form a kite where the centre angle and the external angle sum to 180°. Third, the beautiful one — alternate segment theorem: the angle between a tangent and a chord equals the inscribed angle in the OPPOSITE ('alternate') segment standing on that chord. Proof in three moves: the diameter from the chord's endpoint makes a 90° (Thales), the tangent–radius right angle gives the complement, and same-segment angles close it. Finally, when two chords cross inside, the products of their halves are equal: PA·PB = PC·PD — similar triangles again. These four complete the circle-theorem toolkit.
g10-mathematics-um5-t4.detailed:
Tangent ⟂ radius. The tangent touches at exactly one point T; OT is perpendicular to the tangent line. Proof sketch: any other point P on the tangent line is outside the circle, so OP > r = OT — thus OT is the shortest (perpendicular) distance from O to the line. Converse: a line perpendicular to a radius at its circle point is tangent (any other point of the line lies beyond distance r by Pythagoras). This right angle turns tangent problems into right-triangle problems: e.g. tangent length from external point = √(d² − r²) where d = distance to centre.

Equal tangents (the kite). From external point P, tangents PT₁ and PT₂: right angles at T₁, T₂; OT₁ = OT₂ = r; OP shared → RHS congruence → PT₁ = PT₂ AND ∠T₁PO = ∠OPT₂ (OP bisects) AND ∠T₁OT₂ = 180° − ∠T₁PT₂ (quilateral angle sum with two 90°s). The 'two tangents + two radii' kite is one of geometry's most reused figures. Extension: the incircle of a triangle touches sides in pairs of equal tangents from each vertex — the basis of the 's − a' tangent-length formulas.

Alternate segment theorem. The angle between tangent at A and chord AB equals any inscribed angle standing on AB from the opposite arc: ∠(tangent, AB) = ∠ACB, C on the far arc. Proof: draw diameter AD; ∠ABD = 90° (Thales); in triangle ABD, ∠DAB = 90° − ∠ADB; tangent ⟂ AD gives ∠(tangent, AB) = 90° − ∠DAB = ∠ADB = ∠ACB (same segment on AB). ∎ Use it both ways: to transfer a tangent-chord angle into the circle, or to PROVE a line is tangent by matching the angle. The converse is the standard tangent test in proofs.

Intersecting-chords products. Chords AB and CD crossing at P: PA·PB = PC·PD. Proof: triangles PAC and PDB are similar (vertical angles at P; ∠CAB = ∠CDB, same segment on CB) → PA/PD = PC/PB → cross-multiply. Companion results: secant-secant (external point: PA·PB = PC·PD with full secant lengths) and tangent-secant (PT² = PA·PB — the tangent is the geometric mean). These 'power of a point' products turn geometry into arithmetic: given three of four segments, the fourth falls out of one equation.

Chaining everything: hard exam figures mix theorems — tangent-chord angle → alternate segment → cyclic quad supplement → isosceles radii → done. The meta-strategy: (1) mark every equal arc and its angles; (2) draw radii to tangent points; (3) look for the hidden diameter (Thales); (4) hunt similar triangles for products. Each step needs its theorem named — the reason IS the proof.

commonMistakes: Using the alternate segment angle on the SAME side — it equals the angle in the OPPOSITE segment
Forgetting PB = PA + AB in tangent-secant problems (whole secant × external part)
Assuming the tangent-chord angle equals the central angle (it equals the INSCRIBED one; central is double)
Drawing the radius to the tangent point but not marking the 90° — the whole point of the construction
Applying PA·PB = PC·PD to chords that don't actually intersect (need the crossing point P)
Claiming tangent lengths from different external points are equal (only from the SAME point)
Proving tangent ⟂ radius by 'it looks perpendicular' — cite the shortest-distance or converse theorem
applications: Belt drives: the tangent segments between pulleys are the straight belt runs — length via √(d² − (r₁∓r₂)²)
Gear cutting: the involute tooth curve is literally a tangent unwinding from a base circle
Navigation: 'distance to horizon' is a tangent length √((R+h)² − R²) from a ship at height h
CNC/laser cutting: toolpaths enter material along tangents to avoid gouging — tangent geometry in code
Surveying old chains: intersecting-chord products recover missing station distances from crossing sight-lines
g10-mathematics-um5-t4.summary: Tangents bring right angles: tangent ⊥ radius at contact, making external-point problems Pythagorean (t = √(d² − r²)) and forming the equal-tangent kite (∠centre = 180° − ∠external). The alternate segment theorem transfers tangent-chord angles into the circle's inscribed angles, and crossing lines obey power-of-a-point products: PA·PB = PC·PD, PT² = PA·PB. Mastery is chaining these with the Unit-5-t2 angle theorems, each step reason-tagged.
